questionText: Which pair of physical quantities represents the two supplementary quantities in the SI system of units?

options.text: Luminous intensity and amount of substance

explanation: In the SI system, alongside the seven fundamental quantities, plane angle (measured in radian, rad) and solid angle (measured in steradian, sr) are defined as the two supplementary quantities.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (SI Supplementary Units)

questionText: How many significant figures are present in the measured value 0.004050 m?
explanation: Leading zeros before the first non-zero digit (0.00) are only placeholders and are not significant. In 0.004050, the digits 4, 0, 5, and the trailing zero after the decimal point are all significant, giving 4 significant figures.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Significant Figures)

questionText: A parsec (pc) is defined in astronomy using stellar parallax. Approximately how many light-years equal 1 parsec?
explanation: 1 parsec = 3.0857 × 10^16 m and 1 light-year = 9.46 × 10^15 m. Dividing 3.0857 × 10^16 by 9.46 × 10^15 gives approximately 3.26 light-years.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Astronomical Distance Units)

questionText: What is the dimensional formula of dynamic coefficient of viscosity (η), defined by viscous force F = η A (dv/dx)?
explanation: From F = η A (dv/dx), η = F / [A (dv/dx)]. Substituting dimensions: [F] = [M^1 L^1 T^-2], [A] = [L^2], and [dv/dx] = [L T^-1]/[L] = [T^-1]. Thus [η] = [M^1 L^1 T^-2] / ([L^2][T^-1]) = [M^1 L^-1 T^-1].
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Dimensions of Physical Quantities)

questionText: The kinetic energy of a body is calculated from K = (1/2)mv^2. If the percentage error in measuring mass m is 1.5% and in measuring speed v is 2.5%, what is the maximum percentage error in K?
explanation: For K = (1/2)m^1 v^2, the maximum relative error is ΔK/K = (Δm/m) + 2(Δv/v). Converting to percentages: (ΔK/K) × 100% = 1.5% + 2(2.5%) = 1.5% + 5.0% = 6.5%.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Propagation of Errors)

questionText: In the van der Waals gas equation (P + a/V^2)(V - b) = RT for 1 mole of a gas, where P is pressure and V is volume, what are the SI units of the constant 'a'?
explanation: By the principle of dimensional homogeneity, a/V^2 must have the same unit as pressure P (N/m^2). Since V has unit m^3, V^2 has unit m^6. Therefore, the unit of a = (N/m^2) × m^6 = N·m^4.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Principle of Homogeneity)

questionText: A physical quantity X is determined from the relation X = (A^2 B^3) / (C √D). If the percentage errors in measuring A, B, C, and D are 1%, 2%, 3%, and 4% respectively, what is the maximum percentage error in X?
explanation: Using error propagation rules for products and quotients, (ΔX/X)% = 2(ΔA/A)% + 3(ΔB/B)% + 1(ΔC/C)% + (1/2)(ΔD/D)% = 2(1%) + 3(2%) + 3% + 0.5(4%) = 2% + 6% + 3% + 2% = 13%.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Combination of Percentage Errors)

topic: Dimensional Derivation in New Fundamental Units
questionText: If speed of light (c), gravitational constant (G), and Planck's constant (h) are chosen as fundamental quantities, what is the dimensional formula of mass in this system?
explanation: Let [M] = [c]^x [G]^y [h]^z = [L T^-1]^x [M^-1 L^3 T^-2]^y [M^1 L^2 T^-1]^z. Equating powers: for M: -y + z = 1; for L: x + 3y + 2z = 0; for T: -x - 2y - z = 0. Adding the L and T equations gives y + z = 0, so z = -y. Substituting into -y + z = 1 gives 2z = 1 ⇒ z = 1/2, y = -1/2, and x = -2(-1/2) - 1/2 = 1/2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Units and Measurements (Dimensional Derivation in New Fundamental Units)

questionText: What is the magnitude of the vector A = 3i - 4j + 12k in three-dimensional Cartesian space?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Unit Vectors)

questionText: Two non-zero vectors P and Q are mutually perpendicular if and only if:

options.text: Their scalar (dot) product P · Q equals zero
Their scalar product P · Q equals |P||Q|
Their vector (cross) product P × Q equals the null vector

explanation: Since P · Q = |P||Q| cos θ, for two non-zero vectors to be perpendicular (θ = 90°), cos 90° = 0, so P · Q = 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Scalar Product Condition for Orthogonality)

questionText: For what value of the scalar p are the vectors A = 2i + pj + k and B = 4i - 2j - 2k perpendicular to each other?
explanation: For perpendicular vectors, A · B = 0. Computing the dot product: (2)(4) + (p)(-2) + (1)(-2) = 0 ⇒ 8 - 2p - 2 = 0 ⇒ 2p = 6 ⇒ p = 3.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Orthogonal Vectors Parameter)

questionText: Two forces of equal magnitude F act at a point such that the magnitude of their resultant is also F. What is the angle between the two forces?
explanation: By the parallelogram law, R^2 = F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 cos θ. Given R = F: F^2 = 2F^2(1 + cos θ) ⇒ 1 + cos θ = 1/2 ⇒ cos θ = -1/2 ⇒ θ = 120°.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition)

questionText: The displacement x (in metres) of a particle along the x-axis varies with time t (in seconds) as x = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t + 4. At what instants is the instantaneous velocity of the particle zero?
explanation: Instantaneous velocity v = dx/dt = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t^2 - 3t + 2) = 6(t - 1)(t - 2). Setting v = 0 yields t = 1 s and t = 2 s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Calculus in Physics)

topic: Vector Cross Product and Area of Parallelogram
questionText: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are represented by vectors A = i + 2j + 3k and B = 3i - 2j + k. What is the area of the parallelogram in square units?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Vector Cross Product and Area of Parallelogram)

topic: Relation Between Dot and Cross Products
questionText: If two non-zero vectors A and B satisfy |A × B| = √3 (A · B), what is the magnitude of their resultant |A + B|?
explanation: |A × B| = √3 (A · B) implies AB sin θ = √3 AB cos θ, so tan θ = √3 and θ = 60° (since A · B > 0). Then |A + B| = √(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos 60°) = √(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB(1/2)) = √(A^2 + B^2 + AB).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Mathematical Methods (Relation Between Dot and Cross Products)

questionText: Neglecting air resistance and assuming constant acceleration due to gravity, what is the shape of the path followed by an oblique projectile launched near the Earth's surface?

options.text: Ellipse with centre at launch point

explanation: Eliminating time t between x = (u cos θ)t and y = (u sin θ)t - (1/2)gt^2 gives y = x tan θ - [g / (2u^2 cos^2 θ)] x^2, which is a quadratic equation y = ax - bx^2 representing a parabola.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Projectile Trajectory Shape)

questionText: For a given initial speed u on level ground, a projectile achieves the exact same horizontal range R for which pair of launch angles?
explanation: Horizontal range R = (u^2 sin 2θ)/g is identical for complementary launch angles θ and (90° - θ) because sin(2(90° - θ)) = sin(180° - 2θ) = sin 2θ. Since 35° + 55° = 90°, they yield the same range.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Complementary Angles of Projection)

questionText: A ball is projected from level ground with speed 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, what is the maximum height reached by the ball?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Projectile Maximum Height and Range)

questionText: A stone tied to a string of length 0.5 m is whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant speed, completing 2 revolutions per second. What is the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration?
explanation: Angular speed ω = 2πn = 2π(2) = 4π rad/s. Centripetal acceleration a_c = ω^2 r = (4π)^2 × 0.5 = 16π^2 × 0.5 = 8 π^2 m/s^2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Uniform Circular Motion)

questionText: Raindrops are falling vertically downward at 12 m/s relative to the ground. A cyclist rides due east on a level road at 5 m/s. What is the speed of the raindrops relative to the cyclist?
explanation: Velocity of rain relative to cyclist is v_rc = v_r - v_c. Since v_r (vertical, 12 m/s) and -v_c (west, 5 m/s) are mutually perpendicular, |v_rc| = √(12^2 + 5^2) = √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13 m/s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Relative Velocity in Two Dimensions)

questionText: For an oblique projectile launched over horizontal ground, the horizontal range R is equal to 4√3 times the maximum height H attained. What is the angle of projection with the horizontal?
explanation: Using R = (u^2 sin 2θ)/g = (2u^2 sin θ cos θ)/g and H = (u^2 sin^2 θ)/(2g), we have R/H = 4 cot θ. Given R = 4√3 H, 4 cot θ = 4√3 ⇒ cot θ = √3 ⇒ tan θ = 1/√3 ⇒ θ = 30°.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Range to Maximum Height Ratio)

questionText: A bob tied to a inextensible string of length 1.0 m revolves in a horizontal circle as a conical pendulum such that the string makes a constant angle of 60° with the vertical. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, what is its period of revolution?
explanation: The time period of a conical pendulum is T = 2π √(L cos θ / g). Substituting L = 1.0 m, cos 60° = 0.5, and g = 10 m/s^2 gives T = 2π √(0.5 / 10) = 2π / √20 = 2π / (2√5) = (π / √5) s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (Conical Pendulum)

questionText: The position vector of a particle moving in the xy-plane is given by r(t) = (3t)i + (4t - 5t^2)j metres, where t is in seconds. What is the speed of the particle at t = 1 s?
explanation: Velocity vector v(t) = dr/dt = 3i + (4 - 10t)j m/s. At t = 1 s, v(1) = 3i - 6j m/s. Therefore speed |v(1)| = √(3^2 + (-6)^2) = √(9 + 36) = √45 = 3√5 m/s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Motion in a Plane (2D Kinematics with Position Vector)

topic: Inertial Frames and Newton's First Law
questionText: Newton's first law of motion primarily establishes the physical concept of inertia and defines:

options.text: Inertial frames of reference in which an isolated body moves with constant velocity
The proportionality between gravitational mass and universal constant G
Action-reaction pairs acting on the exact same body
Conservation of mechanical energy in non-conservative fields

explanation: Newton's first law defines inertia (resistance to change in velocity) and identifies inertial frames—reference frames in which zero net external force corresponds to zero acceleration.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Inertial Frames and Newton's First Law)

questionText: In a perfectly inelastic head-on collision between two bodies that stick together after impact, what is the value of the coefficient of restitution (e)?
explanation: Coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation) / (relative speed of approach). Since the two bodies stick together after a perfectly inelastic collision, their relative velocity of separation is zero, so e = 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Coefficient of Restitution)

questionText: A 0.20 kg cricket ball travelling horizontally at 15 m/s is hit straight back along its incoming path at 25 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse imparted to the ball by the bat?
explanation: Taking the outgoing direction as positive, initial velocity u = -15 m/s and final velocity v = +25 m/s. Impulse J = Δp = m(v - u) = 0.20 × [25 - (-15)] = 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 N·s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Impulse and Linear Momentum)

questionText: A stationary shell of mass 5 kg explodes into two fragments of masses 2 kg and 3 kg. If the 2 kg fragment flies off with a speed of 18 m/s, what is the recoil speed of the 3 kg fragment?
explanation: Internal explosion conserves total linear momentum. Since initial momentum is zero, m_1 v_1 = m_2 v_2 in magnitude ⇒ 2 × 18 = 3 × v_2 ⇒ v_2 = 36 / 3 = 12 m/s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Conservation of Linear Momentum)

questionText: A force F = (2i + 3j) N acts on a rigid body at a point whose position vector relative to the origin is r = (4i + 2j) m. What is the torque τ about the origin?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Torque of a Coplanar Force)

topic: Work Done by a Variable Force
questionText: A particle moves along the x-axis from x = 0 m to x = 2 m under the action of a variable force F(x) = (6x^2 - 4x + 5) N directed along +x. How much work is done by this force?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Work Done by a Variable Force)

topic: Centre of Mass of Discrete Particles
questionText: Three point masses of 1 kg, 2 kg, and 3 kg are located in the xy-plane at (0, 0), (3 m, 0), and (0, 4 m) respectively. What are the coordinates of the centre of mass of the system?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Centre of Mass of Discrete Particles)

topic: Self-Adjusting Static Friction on an Incline
questionText: A 4 kg block is placed gently on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, where the coefficient of static friction is μ_s = 0.60 (take g = 10 m/s^2). What is the actual frictional force acting on the block?
explanation: Down-slope gravitational component is mg sin 30° = 4 × 10 × 0.5 = 20 N. Limiting static friction is f_s,max = μ_s mg cos 30° = 0.60 × 40 × (√3/2) ≈ 20.78 N. Since mg sin 30° < f_s,max, the block remains at rest and static friction self-adjusts to match the driving force of 20 N.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Laws of Motion (Self-Adjusting Static Friction on an Incline)

questionText: Kepler's second law (a planet's radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time) is a direct consequence of the conservation of:
explanation: Gravitational force is a central force exerting zero torque about the Sun, so angular momentum L is conserved. Since areal velocity dA/dt = L/(2m), constant L guarantees constant areal velocity.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Kepler's Law of Areas)

questionText: Assuming the Earth to be a sphere of uniform mass density, what is the value of acceleration due to gravity g at the exact geometric centre of the Earth?
explanation: Variation of gravity with depth d is g_d = g(1 - d/R). At the centre of the Earth, d = R, so g_d = g(1 - 1) = 0 because gravitational pulls from surrounding mass elements cancel symmetrically.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Gravity at Earth's Centre)

questionText: At what altitude h above the Earth's surface (in terms of Earth's radius R) does the acceleration due to gravity decrease to 1/9 of its value at the surface?
explanation: Using the exact formula g_h = g [R / (R + h)]^2, setting g_h = g/9 gives [R / (R + h)]^2 = 1/9 ⇒ R / (R + h) = 1/3 ⇒ R + h = 3R ⇒ h = 2R.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Variation of Gravity with Altitude)

topic: Escape Velocity vs Critical Orbital Velocity
questionText: What is the ratio of the escape speed (v_e) from the Earth's surface to the critical orbital speed (v_c) of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface?
explanation: Escape speed at the surface is v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR), while critical orbital speed close to the surface is v_c = √(GM/R) = √(gR). Hence v_e : v_c = √2 : 1.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Escape Velocity vs Critical Orbital Velocity)

questionText: Assuming uniform density of the Earth (radius R), if surface gravity is g_0, what is the acceleration due to gravity at a depth d = R/4 below the surface?
explanation: At depth d inside a uniform spherical Earth, g_d = g_0(1 - d/R). Substituting d = R/4 gives g_d = g_0(1 - 1/4) = (3/4)g_0 = 0.75 g_0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Variation of Gravity with Depth)

topic: Binding Energy of an Orbiting Satellite
questionText: A 400 kg satellite revolves in a circular orbit at an altitude h = R above the Earth's surface, where R is the Earth's radius. Given GM/R = 6.25 × 10^7 J/kg, what is the binding energy of the satellite?
explanation: Orbital radius r = R + h = 2R. Binding energy of a satellite in circular orbit is BE = GMm / (2r) = GMm / (4R) = (GM/R) × (m/4) = 6.25 × 10^7 × (400 / 4) = 6.25 × 10^9 J.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Binding Energy of an Orbiting Satellite)

questionText: Two satellites A and B move in circular orbits of radii 4R and 9R respectively around the same planet. If the orbital speed of satellite A is 6.0 km/s, what is the orbital speed of satellite B?
explanation: Critical orbital speed v = √(GM/r) is inversely proportional to √r. Therefore v_B / v_A = √(r_A / r_B) = √(4R / 9R) = 2/3, giving v_B = (2/3) × 6.0 = 4.0 km/s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Gravitation (Orbital Speed Scaling)

questionText: Within the elastic limit of a solid material, Hooke's law states that:

options.text: Longitudinal strain is independent of applied load
Stress is directly proportional to strain
Plastic deformation is completely reversible upon unloading
Stress is inversely proportional to Young's modulus

explanation: Robert Hooke established that for small deformations within the elastic limit, the restoring stress developed inside a body is directly proportional to the fractional deformation (strain).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Hooke's Law)

questionText: The reciprocal of the bulk modulus of elasticity (1/K) of a material is defined as its:
explanation: Compressibility is defined as fractional volume change per unit change in pressure, -ΔV / (V ΔP), which equals the reciprocal of bulk modulus K.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Compressibility)

questionText: A 2.0 m long metallic wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10^-6 m^2 elongates by 1.0 mm when stretched by a tensile force of 400 N within its elastic limit. What is the Young's modulus of the wire?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Young's Modulus Calculation)

questionText: When a cylindrical metal rod is subjected to axial tension, its length increases by 0.20% while its diameter decreases by 0.06%. What is Poisson's ratio (σ) for the metal?
explanation: Poisson's ratio σ = (lateral strain) / (longitudinal strain) = |ΔD/D| / (ΔL/L) = 0.06% / 0.20% = 0.30.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Poisson's Ratio)

questionText: A wire of volume 5.0 × 10^-5 m^3 made of steel (Young's modulus Y = 2.0 × 10^11 Pa) is subjected to a uniform tensile stress of 2.0 × 10^8 Pa. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the wire?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Elastic Strain Energy)

questionText: Two wires A and B made of the same alloy have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and radii in the ratio 2 : 1. When stretched by identical tensile loads within the elastic limit, what is the ratio of their elongations (ΔL_A : ΔL_B)?
explanation: Elongation ΔL = FL / (π r^2 Y). For equal F and Y, ΔL_A / ΔL_B = (L_A / L_B) × (r_B / r_A)^2 = (1/2) × (1/2)^2 = 1/8, i.e., 1 : 8.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Comparison of Wire Elongations)

questionText: For a homogeneous isotropic solid, Young's modulus Y is found to be 2.4 times its modulus of rigidity η. What is the Poisson's ratio σ of the solid?
explanation: Using the standard relation Y = 2η(1 + σ), substituting Y = 2.4η gives 2.4η = 2η(1 + σ) ⇒ 1 + σ = 1.20 ⇒ σ = 0.20.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Mechanical Properties of Solids (Relation Between Elastic Moduli)

questionText: Absolute zero (0 K) on the Kelvin thermodynamic scale corresponds to which temperature on the Celsius scale?
explanation: The Celsius and Kelvin scales are related by T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. Setting T = 0 K yields t = -273.15 °C.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Thermodynamic Temperature Scale)

questionText: When pure liquid water is heated at standard atmospheric pressure from 0 °C to 10 °C, at approximately what temperature does its density reach a maximum?
explanation: Due to anomalous expansion, water contracts upon heating from 0 °C to 4 °C (reaching minimum volume and maximum density at 4 °C) before expanding above 4 °C.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Anomalous Behaviour of Water)

questionText: An isotropic brass cube has a coefficient of linear thermal expansion α = 1.9 × 10^-5 K^-1. What is its coefficient of cubical (volume) expansion γ?
explanation: For small thermal expansions in an isotropic solid, γ = 3α = 3 × 1.9 × 10^-5 K^-1 = 5.7 × 10^-5 K^-1.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Coefficients of Thermal Expansion)

questionText: How much heat energy (in kJ) is needed to convert 50 g of ice at 0 °C completely into water at 20 °C? (Latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 J/g; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Latent Heat and Calorimetry)

questionText: A star radiates approximately as a blackbody with peak spectral emission at wavelength λ_max = 500 nm. Taking Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10^-3 m·K, what is the surface temperature of the star?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Wien's Displacement Law)

questionText: A hot liquid cools from 70 °C to 60 °C in 5 minutes in a room maintained at 25 °C. Using the mean-temperature form of Newton's law of cooling, how much time will it take to cool from 60 °C to 50 °C?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Newton's Law of Cooling)

questionText: Two rods A and B of identical length and cross-sectional area have thermal conductivities 300 W/(m·K) and 100 W/(m·K) respectively, and are joined end-to-end in series with lagged sides. If the free end of A is held at 100 °C and the free end of B at 20 °C, what is the steady-state interface temperature?
explanation: In steady state, heat current through both rods is equal: K_A A(100 - T)/L = K_B A(T - 20)/L ⇒ 300(100 - T) = 100(T - 20) ⇒ 300 - 3T = T - 20 ⇒ 4T = 320 ⇒ T = 80 °C.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Thermal Properties of Matter (Steady-State Conduction in Series Rods)

questionText: Why can sound waves propagating through air NOT undergo polarization?

options.text: Because their speed is much lower than the speed of light
Because air molecules have zero restoring elasticity
Because sound waves in air are longitudinal mechanical waves
Because polarization only occurs in waves with frequencies below 20 Hz

explanation: Polarization restricts oscillations to a specific plane perpendicular to wave propagation and is therefore exclusive to transverse waves; sound in air oscillates parallel to propagation (longitudinal).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Nature of Sound Waves)

questionText: What is the standard frequency range of audible sound waves for a normal young human ear?
explanation: Human hearing spans approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20,000 Hz); frequencies below 20 Hz are infrasonic and above 20 kHz are ultrasonic.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Limits of Audibility)

questionText: A hiker claps loudly in front of a steep rock face and hears the distinct echo 1.5 s later. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, how far away is the rock face?
explanation: The sound travels a round-trip distance 2d in time t = 1.5 s. Hence d = (v × t) / 2 = (340 × 1.5) / 2 = 255 m.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Echo Range Finding)

topic: Temperature Dependence of Speed of Sound
questionText: By what factor does the speed of sound in an ideal diatomic gas change if its temperature is raised from 27 °C to 927 °C (assuming no dissociation)?

options.text: It increases by a factor of √(927/27)
It increases by a factor of √3

explanation: Speed of sound v = √(γRT/M) ∝ √T, where T is absolute temperature in Kelvin. Here T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K and T_2 = 927 + 273 = 1200 K, so v_2 / v_1 = √(1200 / 300) = √4 = 2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Temperature Dependence of Speed of Sound)

questionText: A progressive wave along a string is described in SI units by y(x, t) = 0.04 sin[2π(25t - x/2)]. What is the wave speed along the string?
explanation: Comparing with y = A sin[2π(nt - x/λ)], frequency n = 25 Hz and wavelength λ = 2 m. Wave speed v = nλ = 25 × 2 = 50 m/s.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Progressive Wave Equation)

questionText: A locomotive whistle emits sound of frequency 640 Hz while approaching a stationary commuter on a platform at 20 m/s. Taking the speed of sound in still air as 340 m/s, what apparent frequency does the commuter hear?
explanation: For an approaching source and stationary observer, n' = n [v / (v - v_s)] = 640 × [340 / (340 - 20)] = 640 × (340 / 320) = 2 × 340 = 680 Hz.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Doppler Effect — Approaching Source)

topic: Doppler Effect — Both Source and Observer Moving
questionText: An ambulance siren of frequency 480 Hz moves at 20 m/s toward a car that is simultaneously approaching the ambulance at 12 m/s along the same straight road. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, what frequency is heard by the driver of the car?
explanation: When observer and source approach each other, n' = n [(v + v_o) / (v - v_s)] = 480 × [(340 + 12) / (340 - 20)] = 480 × (352 / 320) = 1.5 × 352 = 528 Hz.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Sound (Doppler Effect — Both Source and Observer Moving)

questionText: High-speed optical communication fibres guide light pulses from core to receiver with negligible attenuation primarily via:

options.text: Diffraction through microscopic pinholes along the core
Chromatic dispersion inside the outer buffer jacket
Total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface
Specular reflection from silvered metallic walls

explanation: In an optical fibre, the core has a higher refractive index than the surrounding cladding; rays striking the boundary above the critical angle undergo repeated total internal reflection.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Optical Fibres)

questionText: What is the optical power (in dioptres) of a thin converging lens of focal length +25 cm in air?
explanation: Optical power P = 1 / f(in metres) = 1 / (+0.25 m) = +4.0 D.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Optical Power of a Lens)

questionText: Monochromatic light travels from vacuum (c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s) into crown glass of absolute refractive index 1.5. How do its speed and frequency behave upon entering the glass?

options.text: Speed reduces to 2.0 × 10^8 m/s while frequency remains unchanged
Frequency increases by 1.5 while speed reduces to 2.0 × 10^8 m/s
Speed remains 3.0 × 10^8 m/s while wavelength increases by 1.5
Both speed and frequency decrease by a factor of 1.5

explanation: Frequency depends solely on the source and stays invariant across media boundaries. Speed inside the medium becomes v = c / n = (3.0 × 10^8) / 1.5 = 2.0 × 10^8 m/s (and wavelength reduces by 1.5).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Refraction and Wave Parameters)

topic: Critical Angle for Total Internal Reflection
questionText: What is the critical angle for a ray of light travelling from a dense transparent crystal of refractive index 2.0 into air (n = 1.0)?
explanation: At the critical angle θ_c, sin θ_c = n_rarer / n_denser = 1.0 / 2.0 = 0.5, which gives θ_c = arcsin(0.5) = 30°.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Critical Angle for Total Internal Reflection)

questionText: A thin convex lens of focal length +20 cm is placed in coaxial contact with a thin concave lens of focal length -30 cm. What is the equivalent focal length of the combination?
explanation: For thin lenses in contact, 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 = 1/20 + 1/(-30) = (3 - 2)/60 = +1/60 cm^-1, so F = +60 cm (converging combination).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Thin Lenses in Contact)

topic: Minimum Deviation in an Equilateral Prism
questionText: A monochromatic ray passing symmetrically through an equilateral prism (A = 60°) suffers a minimum deviation δ_m = 30°. What is the refractive index of the prism material?
explanation: Using the prism formula n = sin[(A + δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2), we get n = sin[(60° + 30°)/2] / sin(30°) = sin 45° / sin 30° = (1/√2) / (1/2) = √2 ≈ 1.414.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Minimum Deviation in an Equilateral Prism)

topic: Lens Maker's Equation in a Liquid Medium
questionText: A thin glass lens of refractive index 1.50 has a focal length of +20 cm in air (n = 1.00). What will be its focal length when completely immersed in a transparent liquid of refractive index 1.25?
explanation: By the lens maker's formula, 1/f_air = (1.50 - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2) = 0.50 K, and 1/f_liq = (1.50/1.25 - 1) K = (1.20 - 1) K = 0.20 K. Dividing gives f_liq / f_air = 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5 ⇒ f_liq = 2.5 × 20 = +50 cm.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Lens Maker's Equation in a Liquid Medium)

questionText: For a dense flint glass prism, the refractive indices for violet, yellow, and red wavelengths are n_v = 1.62, n_y = 1.60, and n_r = 1.58 respectively. What is the dispersive power (ω) of this glass?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Optics (Dispersive Power of Glass)

questionText: According to the principle of quantization of electric charge, every observable net charge Q on an isolated body is an integral multiple of the elementary charge e equal to:
explanation: Any free electric charge satisfies Q = ±ne (n = 0, 1, 2, ...), where the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Quantization of Charge)

questionText: What is the electrostatic field intensity at any interior point inside the bulk metal of an isolated charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?

options.text: Proportional to distance from the surface
Directed radially inward toward the centre of mass

explanation: Free electrons redistribute on the outer surface until all internal electric fields cancel completely; otherwise, residual fields would drive continuous currents, violating equilibrium.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Conductor in Electrostatic Equilibrium)

questionText: Two point charges of +4.0 μC and +9.0 μC are placed 0.30 m apart in free space [take 1/(4πε_0) = 9.0 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2]. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Coulomb's Law in Vacuum)

topic: Gauss's Law with Dipoles and Point Charge
questionText: A closed Gaussian surface encloses two electric dipoles and an isolated point charge of +8.85 μC. Taking ε_0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2), what is the net outward electric flux through the surface?
explanation: Each electric dipole has zero net charge (+q - q = 0), so total enclosed charge Q_enc = +8.85 × 10^-6 C. By Gauss's law, Φ = Q_enc / ε_0 = (8.85 × 10^-6) / (8.85 × 10^-12) = 1.0 × 10^6 N·m^2/C.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Gauss's Law with Dipoles and Point Charge)

questionText: An electric dipole of dipole moment 5.0 × 10^-8 C·m is oriented at 30° to a uniform electric field of magnitude 4.0 × 10^4 N/C. What is the magnitude of the torque acting on the dipole?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Torque on an Electric Dipole)

questionText: Two positive point charges +4 μC and +16 μC are fixed 60 cm apart in vacuum. At what distance from the +4 μC charge along the line segment joining them is the resultant electric field zero?
explanation: Let the null point lie at distance x cm from +4 μC (and 60 - x cm from +16 μC). Equating field magnitudes: 4 / x^2 = 16 / (60 - x)^2 ⇒ 2 / x = 4 / (60 - x) ⇒ 60 - x = 2x ⇒ 3x = 60 ⇒ x = 20 cm.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Electrostatic Null Point)

topic: Axial and Equatorial Fields of a Short Dipole
questionText: For a short electric dipole of dipole moment p, compare the electric field E_a at a distant point r on its axis with the electric field E_e at the same distance r on its equatorial plane:

options.text: |E_a| = |E_e| and the vectors E_a and E_e are perpendicular (90° apart)
|E_a| = 4|E_e| and the vectors E_a and E_e are antiparallel (180° apart)
|E_a| = 2|E_e| and the vectors E_a and E_e are antiparallel (180° apart)
|E_a| = 2|E_e| and the vectors E_a and E_e are parallel (0° apart)

explanation: At large r (r ≫ 2l), E_a = [1/(4πε_0)](2p/r^3) directed along p, while E_e = -[1/(4πε_0)](p/r^3) directed opposite to p. Thus |E_a| = 2|E_e| and the angle between them is 180°.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Electrostatics (Axial and Equatorial Fields of a Short Dipole)

questionText: What is the SI unit of electrical resistivity (specific resistance) ρ of a material?
explanation: From R = ρL/A, resistivity ρ = RA/L, giving SI unit Ω × m^2 / m = Ω·m.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Unit of Electrical Resistivity)

questionText: How does electrical resistivity change when temperature is moderately increased in a pure metallic conductor compared with an intrinsic semiconductor?

options.text: It increases in both the metal and the intrinsic semiconductor
It increases in the metal and decreases in the intrinsic semiconductor
It decreases in the metal and increases in the intrinsic semiconductor
It decreases in both the metal and the intrinsic semiconductor

explanation: In metals, increased thermal agitation shortens relaxation time and raises resistivity; in intrinsic semiconductors, thermal excitation exponentially increases carrier density, lowering resistivity.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Temperature Dependence of Resistivity)

questionText: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10^-6 m^2 carries a steady current of 3.2 A. Given free electron density n = 8.0 × 10^28 m^-3 and e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, what is the drift speed of the electrons?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Electron Drift Speed)

questionText: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor across an ideal 16 V DC source. What is the total current drawn from the source?
explanation: Parallel resistance R_p = (6 × 12) / (6 + 12) = 72 / 18 = 4 Ω. Total equivalent resistance R_eq = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. By Ohm's law, I = V / R_eq = 16 / 8 = 2.0 A.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Series-Parallel Resistor Combination)

questionText: A platinum resistance thermometer coil has resistance 5.0 Ω at 0 °C and 6.0 Ω at 100 °C. What is the mean temperature coefficient of resistance (α) of platinum over this range?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Temperature Coefficient of Resistance)

topic: EMF and Internal Resistance of a Cell
questionText: A cell of EMF E and internal resistance r delivers a terminal voltage of 1.8 V across a 9.0 Ω external resistor, and 1.6 V across a 4.0 Ω external resistor. What are the values of E and r?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (EMF and Internal Resistance of a Cell)

topic: Resistance After Stretching and Joule Power
questionText: A uniform metallic wire of initial resistance 10 Ω is drawn out uniformly so that its length doubles while its total volume remains constant. If this stretched wire is connected across a 20 V ideal battery, what power is dissipated in it?
explanation: At constant volume V = A L, doubling length halves cross-sectional area (A' = A/2), so R' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R = 40 Ω. Power dissipated P = V^2 / R' = 20^2 / 40 = 400 / 40 = 10 W.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Electric Current Through Conductors (Resistance After Stretching and Joule Power)

questionText: Unlike electrostatic field lines which begin on positive charges and terminate on negative charges, magnetic field lines of a bar magnet always:

options.text: Form closed continuous loops running north-to-south outside and south-to-north inside the magnet
Exist only outside the ferromagnetic material of the magnet
Intersect at the neutral points along the equatorial axis
Originate at the north pole and terminate permanently at the south pole

explanation: Because isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist (∇·B = 0), magnetic field lines always form closed loops continuing from the south pole to the north pole inside the magnet.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Properties of Magnetic Field Lines)

questionText: Which of the following is the standard SI unit of magnetic dipole moment?
explanation: Magnetic dipole moment m = I A (current × area) has SI unit ampere-metre squared (A·m^2), which is also equivalent to joule per tesla (J/T).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Magnetic Dipole Moment Unit)

topic: Magnetic Moment of a Bar Magnet
questionText: A short bar magnet has pole strength 15 A·m and magnetic length (2l) equal to 8.0 cm. What is the magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment?
explanation: Magnetic dipole moment m = q_m × (2l) = 15 A·m × 0.08 m = 1.2 A·m^2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Magnetic Moment of a Bar Magnet)

questionText: At a certain geomagnetic station on Earth, the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field (B_H) is equal in magnitude to its vertical component (B_V). What is the angle of dip (δ) at that location?
explanation: Since tan δ = B_V / B_H, having B_V = B_H gives tan δ = 1, and therefore the angle of dip δ = 45°.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Earth's Magnetic Inclination (Dip))

topic: Axial Magnetic Field of a Short Dipole
questionText: A short bar magnet of magnetic dipole moment 2.5 A·m^2 lies along its axis. Taking μ_0 / (4π) = 10^-7 T·m/A, what is the magnitude of its magnetic field at a distance r = 0.50 m along the axial line from its centre?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Axial Magnetic Field of a Short Dipole)

topic: Potential Energy and Work in Rotating a Magnet
questionText: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 0.40 A·m^2 rests in stable equilibrium (θ = 0°) in a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T. How much external work must be done to rotate it quasi-statically through 120° from this position?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Magnetism (Potential Energy and Work in Rotating a Magnet)

questionText: Which of the following regions of the electromagnetic spectrum has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency?
explanation: In order of decreasing wavelength (increasing frequency): radio > microwave > infrared > visible > ultraviolet > X-rays > gamma rays.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (Electromagnetic Spectrum Ordering)

questionText: In a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in free space, how are the electric field vector E, magnetic field vector B, and propagation direction oriented?

options.text: B × E points along the direction of energy propagation
E is parallel to propagation while B is perpendicular to propagation
E, B, and propagation direction are mutually perpendicular, with E × B pointing along propagation
E and B are parallel to each other and perpendicular to propagation

explanation: Electromagnetic waves are transverse: E ⊥ B, both are perpendicular to the wave vector k, and E × B gives the direction of wave propagation.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (Transverse Nature of EM Waves)

questionText: Long-distance short-wave (HF, 3 MHz to 30 MHz) radio broadcasts reach receivers beyond the horizon by reflection from which region of Earth's atmosphere?
explanation: Ionized layers of the ionosphere (65 km to 400 km altitude) cause total internal reflection of HF radio waves (3–30 MHz) back to Earth in sky-wave propagation.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (Sky-Wave Propagation)

topic: Electric and Magnetic Field Amplitude Ratio
questionText: A plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum has a peak electric field amplitude E_0 = 120 V/m. Taking c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s, what is its peak magnetic field amplitude B_0?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (Electric and Magnetic Field Amplitude Ratio)

questionText: A television broadcast antenna stands 80 m tall above level ground. Taking Earth's radius R = 6.4 × 10^6 m, what is the maximum line-of-sight horizon distance covered by this tower?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (TV Tower Coverage Distance)

questionText: A transmitting antenna of height 45 m communicates in line-of-sight space-wave mode with a receiving antenna of height 80 m. Taking Earth's radius R = 6.4 × 10^6 m, what is the maximum permissible separation between the two antennas?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Electromagnetic Waves and Communication System (Point-to-Point Space Wave Range)

questionText: At room temperature (300 K), what is the approximate forbidden energy band gap (E_g) of pure crystalline silicon (Si)?
explanation: At 300 K, silicon has a band gap of ~1.1 eV (compared to ~0.72 eV for germanium and ~5.5 eV for insulating diamond).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Forbidden Energy Band Gap)

questionText: When pure tetravalent germanium is doped with a trace amount of trivalent indium (In), what type of extrinsic semiconductor is formed?

options.text: p-type semiconductor with negatively charged mobile ions as majority carriers
Intrinsic semiconductor with equal electron and hole concentrations
p-type semiconductor with holes as majority charge carriers
n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority charge carriers

explanation: Each trivalent indium atom accepts one valence electron to complete four covalent bonds, creating a mobile positively charged hole (acceptor impurity ⇒ p-type).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Extrinsic Doping)

questionText: Intrinsic silicon at 300 K has carrier concentration n_i = 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3. If it is doped with donor atoms so that electron concentration becomes n_e = 4.5 × 10^22 m^-3, what is the thermal-equilibrium hole concentration n_h?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Mass-Action Law in Doped Silicon)

questionText: When an external reverse-bias voltage across a p-n junction diode is increased (well below breakdown), what happens to the depletion region and barrier potential?

options.text: Depletion region narrows and majority diffusion current surges
Depletion region widens while potential barrier drops to zero
Depletion region widens and the effective potential barrier increases
Both depletion width and barrier potential remain unchanged

explanation: Reverse bias pulls majority holes in p-region and electrons in n-region away from the junction, uncovering more immobile ions, widening the depletion layer, and raising the barrier height.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Reverse-Biased p-n Junction)

questionText: How does an NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) thermistor respond to a rise in temperature, and what makes it suitable for sensitive thermometry?

options.text: Its electrical resistance increases linearly at a tiny rate with temperature
Its forbidden energy gap widens rapidly upon heating
Its electrical resistance decreases steeply and nonlinearly with increasing temperature
It generates a spontaneous photo-EMF proportional to light intensity

explanation: NTC thermistors are thermally sensitive metal-oxide semiconductors whose resistance drops sharply with small temperature rises, providing high sensitivity in temperature sensing and control.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Thermistors)

questionText: A silicon diode with knee (barrier) voltage 0.7 V and negligible dynamic forward resistance is connected in series with a 215 Ω resistor across a 5.0 V DC supply in forward bias. What current flows through the resistor?
explanation: With 0.7 V dropped across the forward-biased silicon junction, voltage across the series resistor is V_R = 5.0 - 0.7 = 4.3 V. Hence I = 4.3 / 215 = 0.020 A = 20 mA.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Forward-Biased Diode Series Circuit)

questionText: At 300 K, an intrinsic germanium crystal has intrinsic carrier density n_i = 2.5 × 10^19 m^-3, electron mobility μ_e = 0.38 m^2/(V·s), and hole mobility μ_h = 0.18 m^2/(V·s). Taking e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, what is its electrical conductivity?
explanation: For an intrinsic semiconductor (n_e = n_h = n_i), conductivity σ = e n_i (μ_e + μ_h) = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 2.5 × 10^19 × (0.38 + 0.18) = 4.0 × 0.56 = 2.24 S/m.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 14: Semiconductors (Intrinsic Semiconductor Conductivity)
